The first thing anyone noticed about the new clock in Bellweather Station was that it had no hands. The second thing, which took considerably longer to notice, was that people still looked up at it when they hurried through the doors. They would raise their chins, register the blank white circle, and consult a wrist or a telephone instead. By then they had usually stopped walking. This produced a small, persistent traffic jam beneath the clock, exactly where the architect had drawn a cluster of leisurely figures admiring his proposed improvements to the station. He considered this a vindication.

Mara sold coffee from the kiosk opposite platform three. From six until eleven each morning she watched the confusion, and because people assumed that anyone behind a counter knew how the world worked, she answered questions. No, the clock was not broken. Yes, it had been installed that way. No, she did not know what it meant. A brass plaque was supposed to explain the artwork, but the plaque had been delayed. “Probably coming by train,” said a customer in a green coat. He liked his joke so much that he came back the next morning to tell it again.

On Thursday a little girl asked Mara what time she would give the clock if she could choose. Mara was steaming milk and wanted to say something quick, but the question slipped past the busy part of her mind. “Four twenty,” she said. At four twenty, when she was ten, her father used to knock off work at the bakery and bring home whatever had failed to sell. There might be an apricot tart, or there might be six plain rolls and the solemn responsibility of deciding which one to eat first. She had not thought about that in years.

The girl chose midnight, which she had never seen. Her mother chose half past seven on a Sunday morning, provided nobody needed anything. The man in the green coat, overhearing, said he would take the minute before a horse race whose result he already knew. Mara wrote their answers on the cardboard sleeve of a cup. She could not have said why. Business was slow, the pen was handy, and it seemed discourteous to let three perfectly serviceable times disappear. She set the cup beside the till with a handwritten label: TIMES AVAILABLE FOR THE CLOCK. By noon it was full.

People wrote on receipts, ticket stubs, and the margins of a property brochure somebody had abandoned. One person wanted the instant the bath reached the correct temperature. Another specified nine minutes after the birth of his son, when a nurse finally thought to offer him a chair. Somebody wrote “Tuesday,” crossed it out, and wrote “a better Tuesday.” Mara liked the answers that made little sense to anyone but their authors. “Behind the garage, still light.” “When the soup had barley in it.” She emptied the cup into an old biscuit tin and put it back beside the till.

When the plaque arrived, it explained that the absence of hands challenged the tyranny of scheduled movement. A railway employee fixed it to the wall, checked his watch, and ran for the eight fourteen. Most passengers ignored the plaque. A few read it and looked annoyed. The cup was another matter. People began arriving with their answers already written. Some asked to draw out a stranger’s time in exchange for their own. Mara allowed this, reasoning that she had never formally undertaken to provide archival services. Soon passengers were carrying bits of other people’s afternoons to offices all over town.

One wet morning, the man in the green coat drew a square of yellow paper. He read it twice. “The last time I lifted my daughter,” he said. “Not the last time ever. The last time before she got too big.” He folded the paper and slipped it into his breast pocket. For once he had no joke. Mara gave him his coffee, and he went to stand beneath the clock. Through the window she saw him make a call. She could not hear what he said, though she saw him laugh and then hold the phone away to listen.

Winter came. The station roof leaked into a bucket whose position had to be adjusted according to the wind. A timetable change made everyone furious for a week and grateful for a month. Mara’s father moved to a smaller flat, and on her day off she helped him sort his kitchen. In the back of a drawer they found the scalloped metal cutter he had used for apricot tarts. He wanted to throw it away. She wanted to keep it. Neither expected the other to care, and their surprise became an argument that ended, rather pleasantly, in making pastry.

They ate the tarts standing up because the chairs were stacked in the hall. The pastry was tough. Her father blamed the flour, then the oven, then the general decline of apricots. Mara noticed that he had powdered sugar on one eyebrow. Outside, a delivery lorry reversed in a series of mournful beeps. She thought of the cup at work and understood the appeal of writing down an hour you wished to visit again. What surprised her was how little the hour itself seemed to know about being precious. It went on making crumbs and dirty dishes like any other.

On Monday she opened the kiosk at six. The blank clock glowed faintly in the early dark, and the first train brought a smell of wet wool and cold metal into the station. Before the queue formed, Mara took a till receipt and turned it over. She tried to remember when the tarts had come out of the oven. Three, perhaps, or a quarter past. In the end she wrote, “While the chairs were in the hall.” She folded the receipt once and put it in the cup. A woman bought tea, drew Mara’s slip, and carried it downstairs toward the arriving train.
